title: Partial derivatives and coordinate traces
section: Partial Derivatives ▷ Definition and Geometric Interpretation
terms: partial derivative; independent variable; coordinate trace; partial derivative as slope.

exposition.text:
For f(x, y), f (a, b) = lim [f(a + h, b) − f(a, b)]/h when this limit exists; f is defined by
x h→0 y
holding x fixed. Algebraically, treat all other independent variables as constants. Geometrically,
f is the slope of the tangent to the graph’s trace in the vertical plane y = b.
x
Existence of the partial derivatives at a point alone does not imply continuity or differentiabil-
ity there. For piecewise formulas, compute derivatives at exceptional points from the definition
instead of substituting into a formula valid only elsewhere. A tangent direction to the trace
y = b is (1, 0, f ), whereas the trace x = a has direction (0, 1, f ).
x y
If f = 0, the one-variable mean value theorem makes f constant in x on each connected hor-
x
izontal interval of its domain; disconnected slices need not share that constant. Conversely,
integrating a specified x-partial gives an arbitrary function of the other variables, not just one
numerical constant. A derivative along a path changes every input specified by that path.

The plane x = 1 cuts z = arctan(xy) + x y in a curve. Which vector is tangent to this curve at
(1, 1, 1 + π/4)?
(A) (1, 0, 3/2) (B) (0, 2, 3) (C) (0, 3, 2) (D) (2, 0, 3) (E) (0, 1, 2)

solution.text:
2 2 2
With x held fixed, z = x/(1 + x y ) + x = 3/2 at (1, 1). A tangent direction is (0, 1, 3/2),
y
equivalently (0, 2, 3).

Define f(0, 0) = 0 and f (x, y) = xy/(x + y ) elsewhere. Which statement is true at the origin?
(A) f is differentiable
(B) f is continuous but not differentiable
(C) f = f = 0 but f is discontinuous
x y
(D) f exists but f does not
x y
(E) Neither partial derivative exists

solution.text:
On either coordinate axis, f is zero, so both partial derivatives at the origin are zero.
Along y = x ̸= 0, its value is 1/2, so it is not continuous there.

question.text:

Let f(x, y) = log(x/y) for x, y > 0, and g(x) = f(x, x ). What are f (1, 1) and g (1), respec-
x
tively?
(A) 1, 1 (B) −1, −1 (C) 1, −1 (D) −1, 1 (E) 0, 0

solution.text:
For the partial derivative, hold the independent variable y fixed: f = 1/x, giving 1. Along
x
the specified path, g(x) = log(1/x) = − log x, giving derivative −1. Changing a dependent
input during differentiation computes a path derivative, not the same partial derivative.

question.text:
Let D = {(x, y) : x ̸= 0}. Which statement about a continuously differentiable function on D
with f = 0 everywhere is correct?
x
(A) f must be constant on all of D.
(B) f(−1, 0) = f(1, 0) must hold.
(C) f cannot take both values 0 and 1.
(D) f may equal 0 on x < 0 and 1 on x > 0.
(E) No such function can be continuously differentiable.

solution.text:
The stated piecewise constant function is smooth on D because the excluded line separates
its two components. The mean value theorem forces constancy along each connected hori-
zontal interval in D, but cannot cross the missing point x = 0. Thus zero x-partial does not
identify values on disconnected slices.
